title: Mongols, Medieval Europe and the Americas
bigQuestion: On the eve of 1450, how had Europe, Asia and the Americas each built great societies, and what happened when disaster or conquest struck them?

story.title: The Cart from the Coast
story.kicker: In the late summer of 1348 a wool cart rolls into an English village, and within weeks half the churchyard is fresh earth.
paragraphs: The village has no name that matters. It is a cluster of thatched houses beside a stone church, with strip fields around it and a lord's manor house on the hill. About two hundred people live here. Most of them are serfs, farmers bound to the lord's land, and they have never traveled more than a day's walk from it. In August 1348 a carter comes up the road from the port on the south coast with bolts of cloth and a bad cough. He sells his cloth, drinks at the alehouse and moves on.

Four days later the alehouse keeper's son wakes with a fever. Painful swellings the size of eggs rise in his armpits and neck. Dark spots spread under his skin. He dies on the third day. His mother follows within the week. By Michaelmas, at the end of September, the priest is burying people every morning, and then he is buried too. No one knows why. Some say bad air from the south. Some say God's anger. Some blame strangers or Jews, and in parts of Europe mobs murder them for it.

The disease is what we now call the Black Death, a plague carried by fleas that ride on rats and on people. It came from Asia along the trade routes, reached Sicily on ships in 1347, and crossed to England in the summer of 1348. The cart from the coast brought fleas along with cloth. In this village, as in thousands of others, roughly a third to half of the people will die within a year. Whole families vanish. Fields go unharvested because no one is left to cut the grain.

Yet the village does not disappear. The next spring, the survivors face a new world. The lord needs workers and cannot find enough. A serf who once could not leave now walks to the next manor, where a desperate lord offers wages. The king passes a law to freeze pay at the old rates. Workers ignore it. Within a generation, serfdom in England is dying, and in 1381 peasants march on London to demand their freedom. A plague cart began the end of a world that had lasted five hundred years.
story.think: The villagers had no way to know that fleas spread the disease. What explanations did they reach for instead, and what harm did some of those explanations cause?

lessons.title: Lords, Knights and Serfs
lessons.mainIdea: After Rome fell, Europe was held together by feudalism: lords gave land to knights in exchange for military service, and serfs worked the land for both.
reading: After the western Roman Empire broke up in the 400s, there was no emperor to build roads, pay soldiers or keep order. Vikings raided from the north, Magyars from the east, and Muslim fleets from the south. Kings were weak and far away. People needed protection close by. Out of that need grew a system historians call *feudalism*.

It worked like a ladder of promises. A king granted a large piece of land to a powerful noble, a *lord*. In return the lord swore loyalty and promised to bring soldiers when the king called. The lord then granted smaller pieces to *knights*, armored fighters on horseback, who swore the same to him. The land a knight or noble held was his fief. Everyone on the ladder owed something to someone above.

At the bottom were the farmers. Most were *serfs*. A serf was not a slave and could not be sold, but he could not leave the lord's land, and his children were serfs too. He farmed strips in the lord's fields, gave the lord part of his crop and worked the lord's own land several days a week. In return the lord let him farm and promised to protect him. The lord's house, the church and the farmers' huts together made up a *manor*, and most manors produced nearly everything they needed.

How do we know? The Domesday Book, a survey that King William of England ordered in 1086, lists thousands of manors, their lords, their plows, their mills and their serfs by number. Court records show serfs fined for missing work or for marrying without permission. Castles, at first wooden towers on earth mounds and later great stone fortresses, still dot the land where lords once ruled. Feudal Europe left a lot of paper and a lot of stone.

words.d: the medieval system in which lords gave land in exchange for loyalty and military service
a noble who held land from the king and ruled the people on it
an armored soldier on horseback who served a lord in exchange for land
a farmer bound to a lord's land, who could not leave it
a lord's estate: his house, the village, the church and the fields

look.title: One Week on the Manor
look.text: Picture a serf named Wat in the year 1200. Monday and Tuesday he plows the lord's field. Wednesday to Saturday he works his own strips. He owes the lord a tenth of his harvest, and the church another tenth. He must grind his grain at the lord's mill and pay for it. He may not marry off his daughter without the lord's leave. In return, when raiders come, he and his family shelter inside the castle walls.
look.prompt: What did Wat get from this deal, and what did he give up? Was it a fair trade in a world without police or an army?

check.q: Why did feudalism develop in Europe?
choices: There was no strong central government to protect people from raiders
Farmers wanted to own more land
check.why: With Rome gone and Vikings and others raiding, people needed protection from a lord nearby.

check.q: How was a serf different from a slave?
choices: A serf could leave whenever he wanted
A serf owned the land he farmed
A serf could not be sold, though he was bound to the land
A serf did not have to work
check.why: Serfs were tied to the manor and owed labor, but they could not be bought and sold like property.

check.q: What does the Domesday Book tell historians?
choices: The number of manors, mills, plows and serfs in England in 1086
The names of every king of Europe
check.why: William's survey counted the wealth of England manor by manor, giving a detailed picture of feudal life.

lessons.title: The Church and Its Cathedrals
lessons.mainIdea: The Catholic Church was the one institution that reached every village in western Europe, and its cathedrals were the tallest buildings anyone had ever seen.
reading: In feudal Europe, kingdoms came and went, but one thing was the same in every village: the Church. Nearly everyone in western Europe was a Catholic Christian. The parish priest baptized babies, married couples and buried the dead. The Church ran the only schools and hospitals. It collected a tax of one tenth of everyone's income, the tithe. Monasteries, communities of monks, copied books by hand and kept farming skills and Latin learning alive when few others could read.

At the top stood the *pope* in Rome, whom Catholics saw as the head of the Church on earth. Popes crowned emperors and sometimes fought with kings over who could appoint bishops. A pope's strongest weapon was *excommunication*, cutting a person off from the Church and its sacraments. For a believer, that meant fear for his soul. In 1077 a German emperor stood barefoot in the snow for three days to beg a pope's forgiveness.

In the 1100s and 1200s, towns competed to build the grandest church. A *cathedral* was the church of a bishop, and the new style, later called Gothic, used pointed arches and outside supports called flying buttresses to raise walls higher than ever. That let builders fill the walls with huge windows of colored glass. The cathedral at Chartres in France, finished in the 1220s, still has most of its original glass, telling Bible stories to people who could not read.

A cathedral took generations. Masons, carpenters and glassmakers worked their whole lives on one building and died before it was done. The money came from the tithe, from gifts of nobles, and from pilgrims who paid to see holy relics. Some people grumbled about the cost while they went hungry. But when a farmer walked into a cathedral, he stood in the largest indoor space he would ever see, filled with colored light. That was the point.

words.d: the bishop of Rome, head of the Catholic Church
the Church's punishment of cutting a person off from its sacraments and community
the main church of a bishop, usually the largest church in a region
a community where monks live, pray, work and study apart from the world

look.title: Stone Reaching Up
look.text: Stand inside a Gothic cathedral. The ceiling is more than a hundred feet up, held by thin stone ribs. The walls seem to be mostly glass: red, blue and gold, showing saints and kings. Outside, stone arms lean against the walls to keep them from pushing outward. Every farm and shop in the region paid something toward this.
look.prompt: Why might people who lived in one-room huts be willing to pay for a building like this? What did it give them?

check.q: Why was the Church so powerful in feudal Europe?
choices: It reached every village and ran schools, hospitals and records
check.why: The Church was the one institution present everywhere and touched every stage of life.

check.q: What did flying buttresses make possible?
choices: Higher walls with room for huge windows
check.why: Outside supports carried the weight, so walls could rise higher and be filled with glass.

check.q: Why was excommunication such a strong weapon?
choices: It took away a person's land
It sent soldiers against the person
Believers feared losing their soul without the Church's sacraments
It forced a person to leave Europe
check.why: Even an emperor begged forgiveness in the snow rather than remain cut off from the Church.

lessons.title: The Crusades
lessons.mainIdea: For two centuries European knights fought wars to take Jerusalem from Muslim rule; they failed in the end, but the wars changed trade and learning in Europe.
reading: Jerusalem is holy to Jews, Christians and Muslims. Muslim rulers had held it since 638, and for centuries Christian pilgrims visited without much trouble. In the 1000s a new group, the Seljuk Turks, took over the region and defeated the Byzantine army. The Byzantine emperor asked the pope for help. In 1095 Pope Urban II gave a speech in France calling on knights to march east, free the holy city and win forgiveness for their sins. The crowd shouted that God willed it.

Tens of thousands went. The armies of the First *Crusade* captured Jerusalem in 1099 and massacred many of its Muslim and Jewish people. The crusaders set up small kingdoms along the coast. In 1187 the Muslim leader Saladin retook Jerusalem. He spared most of the city's people, and even his enemies wrote of his fairness. More crusades followed for a century, but none won Jerusalem back for long. In 1204 one crusader army never reached the Holy Land at all; it attacked and looted Constantinople, a Christian city, instead.

The crusaders also attacked at home. On their way east in 1096, some bands murdered Jews in cities along the Rhine River. That pattern of violence against Jewish communities returned during the plague and for centuries after. Muslims, Jews and Byzantine Christians all wrote accounts of the crusades, and their view was very different from the knights' songs. Historians read all of them.

The crusades failed at their goal, but they had effects no one planned. Italian cities like Venice and Genoa grew rich shipping soldiers and supplies and bringing back spices, silk and sugar. Europeans tasted goods from the East and wanted more. Scholars in contact with the Muslim world brought back Arabic books on math, medicine and Greek philosophy. Kings who taxed for the wars grew stronger, and many nobles who went east never came home.

words.d: one of a series of wars from 1095 to the 1200s in which European Christians tried to take the Holy Land
the killing of many people who cannot defend themselves
the region around Jerusalem, sacred to Jews, Christians and Muslims

look.title: Two Views of Jerusalem
look.text: A Christian chronicler who was with the army in 1099 described crusaders wading in blood in the streets and mosques of Jerusalem and gave thanks to God for the victory. A Muslim historian, Ibn al-Athir, writing about a century later, listed the same killings, the looting of the holy sites, and the refugees who reached Baghdad weeping and begging the caliph for help.
look.cite: A Latin chronicle of the First Crusade, about 1100, and Ibn al-Athir, The Complete History, about 1230 (both paraphrased)
look.prompt: The two writers agree on what happened but not on what it meant. How should a historian use two sources like these?

check.q: What did Pope Urban II ask knights to do in 1095?
choices: March east and take Jerusalem from Muslim rule
check.why: His speech launched the First Crusade, promising forgiveness of sins to those who went.

check.q: What happened in 1204 that shocked many Christians?
choices: A crusader army looted the Christian city of Constantinople
Jerusalem was destroyed by an earthquake
check.why: The Fourth Crusade never reached the Holy Land and sacked the Byzantine capital instead.

check.q: Which was an unplanned result of the crusades?
choices: Europe gave up trade with the East
Italian port cities grew rich and Europeans wanted eastern goods
check.why: Venice and Genoa profited from shipping, and demand for spices, silk and sugar grew.

lessons.title: The Black Death
lessons.mainIdea: The plague of 1347 to 1351 killed roughly a third or more of Europe's people, and the labor shortage it left behind helped break feudalism.
reading: The *plague* began in Central Asia and traveled the trade routes the Mongols had opened. In 1347 ships from the Black Sea brought it to Sicily. By 1348 it was in Italy, France, Spain and England. By 1351 it had reached Russia and Scandinavia. Trade had connected the world, and the connection carried death as well as silk.

The disease is caused by a bacterium carried by fleas that live on rats. Fleas jumped from dying rats to people. A second form spread directly from person to person by coughing. No one in 1348 knew any of this. Scientists confirmed the bacterium in the 1890s, and in the 2000s they found its DNA in the teeth of plague victims dug from medieval cemeteries. That is how we know the killer's name today.

The count is rough, because medieval records are patchy, but historians estimate that between a third and half of Europe's people died within about four years. Some villages lost everyone. In Florence, the writer Giovanni Boccaccio described dead bodies piled in the streets and neighbors who abandoned each other. Records of English manors show fields left empty and rents unpaid. Some people turned to extreme religion, whipping themselves in the streets. Others blamed Jewish communities and killed thousands in Germany and elsewhere.

Then came a surprise. With so few workers left, a serf who survived could demand wages, or walk to a lord who would pay them. In 1351 the English parliament passed a law ordering pay frozen at the old rates. It did not work. When the government tried to raise taxes in 1381, English peasants rose in revolt and marched into London. The revolt was crushed, but serfdom kept fading. A century after the plague, most English farmers were free tenants paying rent, not serfs owing labor.

words.d: a deadly disease that spreads fast through a population; the Black Death was bubonic plague
a tiny living thing, too small to see, that can cause disease
a time when there are not enough workers for the jobs that need doing

look.title: A Writer in Florence, 1348
look.text: Boccaccio wrote that the swellings appeared first in the groin or armpit, some as large as an apple, and that almost everyone with them died within three days. He said that brother abandoned brother, and often wife abandoned husband, and, hardest of all to believe, that fathers and mothers refused to visit or care for their own children as if they were strangers.
look.cite: Giovanni Boccaccio, The Decameron, introduction, about 1350 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Boccaccio wrote this for readers who had lived through the plague. What does his account tell us that a list of death counts cannot?

check.q: How did the plague reach Europe?
choices: Along trade routes, arriving by ship in Sicily in 1347
Crusaders brought it from Jerusalem in 1099
check.why: The disease traveled from Central Asia on the trade routes and landed in Sicily on Black Sea ships.

check.q: How do scientists today know what caused the Black Death?
choices: They found the bacterium's DNA in the teeth of plague victims
check.why: DNA from medieval cemeteries confirmed the plague bacterium identified in the 1890s.

check.q: Why did the plague help end serfdom in England?
choices: Lords freed serfs out of kindness
Workers were so scarce that survivors could demand wages and leave their lords
check.why: The labor shortage gave farmers bargaining power, and laws to freeze wages failed.

lessons.title: The Great Charter of 1215
lessons.mainIdea: Magna Carta forced an English king to admit that even he was under the law, an idea that later shaped the United States Constitution.
reading: King John of England was losing. He had lost his lands in France in war, and to pay for more war he squeezed his barons, the great lords, for money. He seized land, demanded huge fees when a noble inherited, and jailed men without trial. He also quarreled with the pope, who cut England off from church services for years. By 1215 the barons had had enough. They raised an army and took London.

In June 1215, in a meadow beside the Thames River called Runnymede, John met the barons and put his seal on a long document in Latin. We call it *Magna Carta*, the Great Charter. Most of its sixty-some clauses were about the barons' own complaints: inheritance fees, forests, fish traps in the river. But a few clauses said something bigger. The king could not take new taxes without the consent of his great council. And no free man could be jailed, stripped of property or exiled except by the judgment of his peers or the law of the land.

John never meant to keep it. Within months the pope declared the charter void and war began again. But John died in 1216, and his young son's advisers reissued the charter to win support. Kings confirmed it again and again over the next century. Each time, the idea sank deeper: the king rules under the law, not above it. The great council grew into Parliament, which held the power over taxes.

Five hundred years later, English colonists in America knew Magna Carta well. When they said no taxation without representation, they were pointing to it. When the United States Constitution promised that no one could lose life, liberty or property without due process of law, it echoed the clause sealed at Runnymede. A copy of the 1215 charter is displayed in the National Archives in Washington, next to the Declaration of Independence.

words.d: the Great Charter of 1215 in which King John agreed that the king was under the law
a great lord who held land directly from the king
a written document that grants or guarantees rights
fair legal steps that must be followed before the government can punish a person

look.title: The Clause That Lasted
look.text: One clause of Magna Carta promises that no free man shall be arrested, imprisoned, stripped of his property, outlawed or exiled, or harmed in any way, except by the lawful judgment of his equals or by the law of the land. Another clause promises that the king will sell justice to no one, and will not deny or delay it to anyone.
look.cite: Magna Carta, clauses 39 and 40, 1215 (paraphrased from the Latin)
look.prompt: The clause says free man. Most English people in 1215 were serfs, not free. Who was left out, and how did the idea grow to include more people later?

check.q: Why did the barons rebel against King John?
choices: He refused to go on crusade
He seized land, demanded huge fees and jailed men without trial to pay for war
He wanted to move the capital
check.why: John's demands for money and his arbitrary punishments drove the great lords to take up arms.

check.q: What big idea did Magna Carta establish?
choices: The king rules under the law, not above it
check.why: Clauses on taxes and lawful judgment limited the king's power, and later kings confirmed them.

check.q: How did Magna Carta influence the United States?
choices: Its promise of judgment by law became the idea of due process in the Constitution
check.why: Colonists pointed to the charter, and the Constitution's due process clause echoes clause 39.

lessons.title: Genghis Khan Unites the Steppe
lessons.mainIdea: Genghis Khan united the horse-riding tribes of Mongolia and built the largest connected land empire in history, at a terrible cost to those who resisted.
reading: North of China stretches the *steppe*, a sea of grass too dry for farming. Its people lived by herding horses, sheep and cattle, moving with the seasons and living in round felt tents. Boys learned to ride and shoot a bow before they could plow. The tribes fought each other constantly. Around 1162 a boy named Temujin was born there. His father was poisoned by enemies when Temujin was about nine, and his family was left to starve on the steppe.

Temujin survived by building alliances, and by 1206 he had united all the Mongol tribes. They gave him the title *Genghis Khan*, universal ruler. He organized his army in groups of ten, a hundred, a thousand and ten thousand, mixing the tribes so that loyalty went to him, not to old clans. He promoted men for skill, not birth. His riders could travel fifty miles or more a day, each with several spare horses, and shoot accurately from the saddle at a gallop.

Then he turned outward. Cities that surrendered were spared and taxed. Cities that resisted were destroyed as a warning, and Mongol armies killed on a scale that horrified every writer of the age. By his death in 1227 Genghis ruled from northern China to the Caspian Sea. His sons and grandsons pushed on into Russia, Persia and eastern Europe. In 1258 they took Baghdad, killed the caliph and ended the Abbasid caliphate. In 1279 his grandson Kublai Khan finished conquering China and ruled it as emperor.

At its height the Mongol Empire stretched from Korea to Hungary, the largest connected land empire ever. It was really four related empires ruled by Genghis's descendants. Historians debate how to weigh the destruction against what came after. Persian and Chinese writers recorded the massacres in detail. But the same writers, a generation later, worked for Mongol rulers who paid for observatories, histories and hospitals.

words.d: the vast dry grassland of Central Asia, home to horse-riding herders
the title of Temujin, who united the Mongols in 1206 and founded their empire
a Mongol or Turkic word for ruler

look.title: The Mongol Century
rows: Kublai Khan rules all of China
look.prompt: How many years passed from Genghis's title to the fall of Baghdad? What let a people of herders conquer so much so fast?

check.q: How did Genghis Khan keep his army loyal to himself rather than to old tribes?
choices: He mixed the tribes into units of ten and promoted men for skill
He let each tribe fight separately
check.why: Mixed units and promotion by ability broke old clan loyalties and tied men to the khan.

check.q: What happened to a city that resisted the Mongols?
choices: It was usually destroyed as a warning to others
It was made the new capital
check.why: Cities that surrendered were spared; those that fought were often wiped out.

check.q: What ended in 1258 when the Mongols took Baghdad?
check.why: The Mongols killed the caliph, ending the Abbasid line that had ruled from Baghdad since 762.

lessons.title: The Mongol Peace and Marco Polo
lessons.mainIdea: Under Mongol rule the roads across Asia became safe enough for merchants and travelers like Marco Polo, and ideas, goods and disease all moved faster.
reading: Once the conquests slowed, the Mongols wanted the wealth that trade brought. They set up relay stations about a day's ride apart across Asia, with fresh horses and food for official messengers. A message could cross the empire in weeks. Merchants with a Mongol pass could travel under protection. Historians call this period, roughly 1250 to 1350, the *Pax Mongolica*, the Mongol Peace. A saying of the time claimed a girl with a bag of gold could walk across the empire unharmed.

In 1271 a seventeen-year-old from Venice named Marco Polo set out with his father and uncle, who were merchants. They crossed deserts and mountains for more than three years to reach the court of Kublai Khan in China. Marco stayed about seventeen years, working for the khan and traveling across China. He came home in 1295. Captured in a war between Venice and Genoa, he dictated his story in prison to a writer of romances.

His book described things Europeans found hard to believe: a city with canals and twelve thousand bridges, coal burned as fuel, paper money printed by the government, and a postal system faster than anything in Europe. Some readers called him a liar. Some historians still argue about which parts he saw himself and which he heard from others. But much of what he wrote checks out against Chinese records, and his book became a favorite of a later sailor named Christopher Columbus.

The Mongol Peace carried more than merchants. Chinese inventions such as gunpowder, printing and the compass moved west along the same roads. So did the plague in the 1340s. And the peace did not last. The Mongol khanates fought each other, China threw out its Mongol rulers in 1368, and the roads grew dangerous again. Europeans who had tasted Asian silk and spices now looked for another way to reach them, by sea.

words.d: the Mongol Peace, roughly 1250 to 1350, when Mongol rule made travel across Asia safer
a post along a road where messengers could get fresh horses and food
printed notes used instead of coins, first used by governments in China

look.title: Money Made of Paper
look.text: Marco Polo described how the Great Khan's mint took the bark of mulberry trees, made it into sheets like paper, cut them into pieces of different sizes and stamped each with the khan's seal. He said the khan paid for everything with this money, and that anyone who refused it could be put to death, so everyone accepted it as if it were gold.
look.prompt: Why would a piece of paper work as money in China? What made a Venetian reader in 1300 refuse to believe it?

check.q: What was the Pax Mongolica?
choices: A treaty between the Mongols and the pope
A period when Mongol rule made travel across Asia safer
check.why: Relay stations, passes and protected roads made the century from about 1250 to 1350 a time of easier trade.

check.q: Why did some Europeans call Marco Polo a liar?
choices: He described things like paper money and coal that seemed impossible to them
He claimed to be the khan
check.why: China's cities, money and inventions were beyond anything Europeans had seen.

check.q: What was one harmful thing that traveled the Mongol roads?
check.why: The same routes that carried goods and inventions carried the Black Death westward.

lessons.title: Japan Under the Shoguns
lessons.mainIdea: In Japan a military ruler called the shogun held real power while the emperor reigned in name, and samurai warriors served their lords much as knights did in Europe.
reading: Japan is a chain of mountainous islands off the coast of Asia. It borrowed writing, Buddhism and government ideas from China and Korea, but it was never conquered by them. For centuries an emperor in the city of Kyoto stood at the top of Japanese society, seen as descended from the sun goddess. But by the 1100s the emperor had little real power. Great families with private armies fought each other for control.

In 1185 a warrior named Minamoto Yoritomo won that war. In 1192 the emperor gave him the title *shogun*, which means great general. The emperor kept his throne and his ceremonies, but the shogun ran the country from his own headquarters. For nearly seven hundred years, until 1868, shoguns ruled Japan in the emperor's name. Under the shogun, lords called *daimyo* held land and kept armies of warriors called *samurai*.

A samurai was much like a European knight. He fought on horseback with bow and sword, served a lord, and received land or rice in return. He followed a code of loyalty and honor that later got the name bushido, the way of the warrior. A samurai who failed his lord was expected to take his own life. Samurai families also produced poets, painters and Buddhist thinkers, and the tea ceremony grew up in their world.

The shoguns faced their greatest test from the Mongols. Kublai Khan sent fleets to invade Japan in 1274 and again in 1281, with tens of thousands of soldiers. Both times the samurai fought on the beaches, and both times huge storms wrecked the Mongol ships. The Japanese called those storms kamikaze, divine winds. Japan stayed independent, but the shogun could not reward his samurai with new land, because there was none to give, and his rule weakened.

words.d: the military ruler of Japan who held real power while the emperor reigned in name
a Japanese lord who held land and commanded samurai
a Japanese warrior who served a lord in exchange for land or rice

look.title: Knight and Samurai
look.text: A knight in France in 1250 and a samurai in Japan in 1250 have never heard of each other. Both fight on horseback for a lord. Both hold land in exchange for service. Both follow a code of honor. Both live in a country where the king or emperor is weak and local lords are strong.
look.prompt: Two societies with no contact built such similar systems. What problem were both of them solving?

check.q: Who held real power in Japan after 1192?
check.why: The emperor kept his ceremonies, but the shogun, the great general, actually ran the country.

check.q: In what way was a samurai like a European knight?
choices: Both served a lord in exchange for land and followed a code of honor
Both were paid in paper money
check.why: Both were mounted warriors bound by loyalty to a lord who gave them land or income.

check.q: What stopped the Mongol invasions of Japan in 1274 and 1281?
choices: The Mongols ran out of horses
The Chinese navy sank the fleet
Samurai resistance and huge storms that wrecked the Mongol ships
check.why: The samurai held the beaches and storms, later called kamikaze, destroyed the fleets.

lessons.title: The Maya
lessons.mainIdea: In the rain forests of Central America the Maya built stone cities, invented a full writing system and tracked the sky with a calendar more exact than Europe's.
reading: In what is now Guatemala, Belize, southern Mexico and Honduras, the *Maya* built cities in the jungle. Their greatest period ran from about 250 to 900 CE. Cities such as Tikal and Copan held tens of thousands of people, with stone pyramids taller than any building in Europe at the time, plazas, palaces and ball courts. Each city had its own king. They traded with each other and fought each other, like the city-states of Greece.

The Maya are the only people of the ancient Americas known to have had a full writing system. Their *glyphs*, picture-like signs, could spell any word in their language. They carved them on stone monuments and wrote them in folding books of bark paper. For a long time no one could read them. Scholars cracked the code mainly in the second half of the 1900s. Now we can read the names of Maya kings and the dates of their battles.

Maya astronomers watched the sky for generations and wrote down what they saw. They tracked the planet Venus so closely that their tables were off by only a day or two in a century. They used a symbol for zero and a place-value number system, centuries before Europe learned one. They kept several calendars at once, including one that counted every day from a starting point more than three thousand years before their time.

Around 900 the great cities of the south were abandoned. Historians still argue why. Evidence points to long droughts, recorded in lake mud and cave stones, along with overuse of the forest, war between cities and kings who lost their people's trust. But the Maya did not vanish. Cities in the north, like Chichen Itza, thrived for centuries more. Today about six million Maya people live in Central America and speak Maya languages.

words.d: the people of Central America who built stone cities and a writing system from about 250 CE onward
a carved or painted sign in a writing system
a long period with little or no rain

look.title: Cracking a Code
look.text: For a century, scholars stared at Maya carvings and could not read them. Some said the glyphs were only pictures of gods. Then a young scholar noticed that some signs seemed to stand for sounds, not ideas. Working with Maya languages still spoken today, researchers matched signs to syllables. Suddenly the stones began to tell stories: this king was born, that city was conquered.
look.prompt: Why did it matter that Maya languages are still spoken? What would be lost if a writing system's language had died?

check.q: What makes the Maya unique among ancient peoples of the Americas?
choices: They had a full writing system that could spell any word
check.why: Maya glyphs are the only complete writing system known from the ancient Americas.

check.q: What evidence supports drought as a cause of the Maya collapse around 900?
choices: Layers in lake mud and cave stones that record dry years
Maya kings wrote that it rained too much
check.why: Natural records of rainfall show long droughts around the time the southern cities emptied.

check.q: Which is true of the Maya today?
choices: They only lived in Chichen Itza

check.why: The southern cities were abandoned, but Maya people and languages continue.

lessons.title: The Aztec and Their Island City
lessons.mainIdea: The Aztec built Tenochtitlan on a lake and ruled central Mexico through conquest and tribute, feeding a city of about two hundred thousand from floating farms.
reading: According to their own history, the Mexica, whom we call the *Aztec*, were wanderers who arrived late in the Valley of Mexico. The good land was taken. In 1325 they settled on a swampy island in Lake Texcoco, where, their story said, they saw an eagle on a cactus. That image is on the flag of Mexico today. On that island they built *Tenochtitlan*, which by 1500 was one of the largest cities in the world, with about two hundred thousand people.

Feeding a city on a lake took engineering. The Aztec built *chinampas*, raised fields made by piling mud and plants in the shallow water and fencing them with willow trees. Farmers could take several harvests of corn, beans, squash and chilies from a chinampa every year. Stone causeways with bridges linked the island to the shore, and an aqueduct carried fresh water from springs. Canoes moved through canals, and a market in the district of Tlatelolco drew tens of thousands of people a day.

In 1428 the Aztec joined two neighboring cities in an alliance and began conquering the valley and far beyond. Conquered peoples paid *tribute*: corn, cotton cloth, feathers, cacao beans, gold and captives. Records list every town and exactly what it owed. Aztec religion held that the gods needed human blood to keep the sun moving, and captives from war were sacrificed at the great temple. Neighboring peoples hated Aztec rule, and that hatred mattered later.

Spanish soldiers who saw Tenochtitlan in 1519 wrote that it looked like a dream, with towers rising from the water. Within two years they had destroyed it, with the help of smallpox and tens of thousands of native allies who wanted to end Aztec rule. Mexico City stands on the site today. Archaeologists digging under its streets have found the great temple, and the Aztec tribute lists survive because the Spanish copied them to learn what they could collect.

words.d: the Mexica people who built Tenochtitlan and ruled central Mexico in the 1400s
the Aztec capital, built on an island in Lake Texcoco in 1325, now Mexico City
a raised farm plot built in shallow lake water
goods that a conquered people must pay to their rulers

He said the great market was so large and so orderly, with every kind of goods in its own place, that soldiers who had seen Constantinople and Rome said they had never seen anything like it.

lessons.title: The Inca Road
lessons.mainIdea: In the Andes the Inca ruled the largest empire in the Americas with roads, storehouses and knotted strings, but no wheels, no horses and no writing.
reading: The Andes Mountains run down the west side of South America, and their peaks stand more than twenty thousand feet high. Farming there means building *terraces*, flat steps cut into the mountainsides and walled with stone. Andean peoples grew potatoes and corn on them and raised llamas and alpacas for wool and carrying loads. Around 1438 a ruler of a small mountain kingdom at Cusco, in Peru, began conquering his neighbors. His people were the *Inca*.

In less than a century the Inca ruled from what is now Colombia to Chile, about 2,500 miles along the mountains, with perhaps ten million people. They held it together with roads. Two main highways, one along the coast and one through the mountains, plus side roads, added up to roughly 25,000 miles. Rope bridges swung across gorges. Runners in relays carried messages along the roads at a pace of a hundred miles or more a day. Storehouses along the way held food, cloth and weapons for armies and for villages in bad years.

The Inca had no writing. Instead officials kept records on a *quipu*, a set of colored strings with knots. The position and type of knot recorded numbers: how many people in a village, how many llamas, how much corn in a storehouse. Every family owed the state labor, called mita, for building roads, terraces and cities. In return the state fed people in famine. Conquered peoples were sometimes moved far from home to break up resistance.

Inca builders cut stones so exactly that they fit without mortar, and the walls of Cusco still stand under Spanish churches built on top of them. Machu Picchu, a royal estate high on a ridge, was never found by the Spanish and survives nearly whole. The Inca did all this without iron tools, wheeled carts or horses. When Spanish soldiers arrived in 1532, a civil war and smallpox had already weakened the empire, and the Inca rulers fell within a few years.

words.d: the people of Cusco who built the largest empire in the Americas in the 1400s
a flat step of farmland built into a hillside
an Inca record made of knotted strings, used to keep numbers
the long mountain range along the west side of South America

lessons.title: The World in 1450
lessons.mainIdea: In 1450 the world's great societies were rich, connected within their own regions and unaware of each other across the oceans, and that was about to change.
reading: Stand on the world in 1450 and look around. In China the Ming dynasty rules perhaps a hundred million people, the most on earth. Twenty years earlier its emperor sent Zheng He's giant fleets to India and Africa, then stopped and let the ships rot. In India, Persia and the Ottoman lands, Muslim rulers govern rich cities. Along the Swahili coast and across the Sahara, African traders move gold. In Europe, small kingdoms quarrel, and a German craftsman is perfecting a press that prints with movable type.

Across the Atlantic, the Aztec are expanding in Mexico and the Inca in the Andes. Neither knows the other exists. Neither knows of Europe, and Europe does not know of them. In North America, the great mound city of Cahokia, near what is now St. Louis and Collinsville, Illinois, has already been abandoned for a century. Farming towns line the Mississippi and its branches. No one on either side of the ocean has any idea what is coming.

Compare the societies you have met. All built cities. All had religions that shaped law and daily life. Most had writing; the Inca did not. Europe and Asia had horses, iron, wheels and gunpowder; the Americas did not. Africa, Asia and Europe were linked by routes that carried goods, faiths and, in the 1340s, plague. The Americas were sealed off, so their people had never met the diseases of the other continents. That single fact would decide millions of lives.

Three events within a few years turned the page. In 1453 the Ottoman Turks took Constantinople, ending the Byzantine Empire and pushing Europeans to seek sea routes east. Around 1455 Gutenberg's press printed a Bible, and cheap books spread faster than ever. In 1492 a Genoese sailor who had read Marco Polo sailed west from Spain, looking for Asia, and reached islands no European knew. The next unit begins there.

a large mound-building city near modern St. Louis, on the Illinois side of the river, at its height around 1100
